title: Transactions and ACID
notes: Qualified-claim trap in the source: durability is stated as 'once committed, survives a crash because the log is flushed before commit returns', with isolation described as a spectrum. A summary that says isolation is simply 'transactions do not interfere' drops the qualification. Traps: two-phase commit and MVCC, which the lecture does not cover.

pages.text:
Week 8 — Transactions.

A transaction groups statements into one logical unit. The ACID properties: Atomicity (all or nothing, a failure rolls back every statement), Consistency (a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints), Isolation and Durability.

Isolation is a spectrum, not a switch. Without it a dirty read happens when one transaction reads another's uncommitted change, and a non-repeatable read when the same query returns different rows within one transaction. Stronger isolation levels prevent more anomalies but allow less concurrency.

SERIALIZABLE gives the result of some serial order of the transactions.

Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash. This is achieved with a write-ahead log: the log record is flushed to disk before commit returns, and after a crash the log is replayed to redo committed work.

Example: transfer 100 from account A to B is two updates; atomicity ensures that the debit never happens without the credit.

required_facts.fact: atomicity is all or nothing with rollback on failure
isolation is a spectrum: stronger levels prevent more anomalies but allow less concurrency
dirty read reads another transaction's uncommitted change
log flushed to disk before commit returns, replayed after a crash
transfer example: debit never happens without the credit

forbidden_claims.claim: claims isolation means no interference at all levels
